 News › Learning News › UPSC interview 3 times, CAT 98 percentile: Why Satyam Jain turned down IIM offers after years of civ… UPSC interview 3 times, CAT 98 percentile: Why Satyam Jain turned down IIM offers after years of civil services preparation
 Adhya Sarna Updated: Nov 10, 2026, 07:37 IST Satyam Jain Despite repeated setbacks in the civil services examination, Satyam Jain declined admission to premier institutes in order to guide aspirants, offering a lesson in resilience and strategy.
 Clearing the civil services examination conducted by the Union Public Service Commission ( UPSC ) is the aspiration of millions of young Indians, yet no two candidates travel the same road. Satyam Jain reached the interview stage three times without securing a place on the final merit list. During this period he also appeared for the Common Admission Test ( CAT ) and scored above the 98th percentile. Even so, he chose not to pursue management studies and built a different career. Today he draws on his experience to guide UPSC aspirants.
 Three interviews, no final selection 
 Jain narrated his journey himself in a post on X. He devoted a considerable period to preparation for the UPSC exam and was called for the personal interview on three occasions. Qualifying the Main examination and reaching the interview round is a significant achievement for any candidate. However, missing the final list after getting that far can be deeply disappointing.
 Jain recalls that the final UPSC result, announced on April 16, 2024, did not include his name for the third time. 
 After repeated attempts, the outcome forced him to confront a fundamental question: whether to move beyond UPSC preparation and take another path, or to put his experience to use in a new venture. He chose to think differently.
 A 98+ percentile in CAT, and calls from IIM Lucknow and IIT Delhi 
 While preparing for the civil services, Jain had also kept other options in view. He took the CAT without any special preparation and still secured a percentile above 98. He subsequently received admission calls from the Indian Institute of Management (IIM), Lucknow, and the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Delhi. 
 For a young man from a small village in Uttar Pradesh, these offers opened the door to new possibilities. On one side lay the experience of repeated failure in UPSC; on the other, the chance to study at prestigious institutions.
 Accepting one of these offers would have been the natural step. Yet Jain was weighing more than his own future. The problems and mistakes he had recognised during his preparation continued to challenge other aspirants, and he resolved to put his experience to use for them.
 In his view, hard work alone is not enough in competitive examinations. Effort that lacks direction, a clear strategy and an honest assessment of one's weaknesses may not deliver the desired result even after years of study. Setting aside the option of pursuing an IIM programme, he decided to work for UPSC candidates. He now mentors them through UnderStand UPSC .
 Turning a setback into a business opportunity 
 Jain has said that seeing more than 250 candidates associated with him preparing to join the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration ( LBSNAA ) reassures him that his decision was right. A distinction deserves mention here: a candidate's move to LBSNAA for training follows selection through the civil services process. It is a milestone for those candidates and not a credential of Jain himself.
 His story suggests that failure does not define a person's ability. Rather, it can reveal where a strategy needs to change and how experience can be used to help others.
